sentences.text: Hagryphus giganteus was considered one of the largest oviraptorosaurs, reaching about three meters in length.
Later estimates by Gregory S. Paul in 2010 reduced the size of Hagryphus to eight feet in length and fifty kilograms in weight.
The animal is estimated to have been between 2.4 and 3 meters long and weighed about 50 kilograms.
Oviraptorosaurs, the group to which Hagryphus belongs, are characterized by shortened snouts, toothless jaws, and skulls with elaborate crests of unknown function.
Hagryphus represents the southernmost known oviraptorosaurian dinosaur found in the Americas.
The fossilized hand of Hagryphus is missing the second claw.
Evidence suggests that Hagryphus was feathered, leading some paleontologists to consider it a true bird.
Hagryphus was named in 2005 by paleontologists Lindsay E. Zanno and Scott D. Sampson.
The holotype fossil was discovered in 2002 by Michael Getty in the Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument.
The only known specimen of Hagryphus giganteus consists of an incomplete but articulated left hand and the lower part of the left forearm bone.
The type specimen of Hagryphus is housed in the Utah Museum of Natural History in Salt Lake City.
While some suggest Hagryphus ate eggs due to its toothless jaws, it likely fed on plants or small vertebrates.
Hagryphus lived alongside diverse contemporaries including dromaeosaurids, tyrannosaurids, hadrosaurs, and ceratopsians.
Hagryphus was initially classified as a Caenagnathidae but later reclassified more broadly as an Oviraptorosaurian.
Hagryphus is a monospecific genus of caenagnathid dinosaur that lived 75.95 million years ago in southern Utah.
Hagryphus lived near the western shore of the Western Interior Seaway, which divided North America into Laramidia and Appalachia.
The habitat of Hagryphus was an ancient floodplain featuring wetland swamps, ponds, and lakes bordered by highlands.
The specific function of the elaborate crests on oviraptorosaurs like Hagryphus remains unknown.
